newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Rival states in privatisation drive.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rival states in privatisation drive.

text.p: Brazil's Rio de Janeiro state is beating traditional rival and economic powerhouse Sao Paulo in the privatisation drive, with plans to sell assets ranging from its world famous Maracana soccer stadium to its state bank.

"There will be a boom in state privatisations," said Rodolfo Vasconcelos, privatisation manager with investment bank Bozano, Simonsen which is administering Rio's state bank Banco do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (Banerj) in preparation for privatisation.
"Rio is at the forefront of privatisation and Sao Paulo is now just starting to join in," he said.
In addition to Banerj, Rio de Janeiro is selling off state electricity and gas companies Cerj and CEG, as well as transport firms Conerj, Flumitrens and Metro.
Overall, Rio has earmarked 21 of 26 state-owned companies for sale, concession or liquidation, with many due to be sold off this year.
SAO PAULO PRIVATISATION SLOWER BUT MORE AMBITIOUS
Although Sao Paulo's privatisation programme has been off to a slow start it is more ambitious with the state hoping to raise more than $20 billion as opposed to Rio's $5 billion.
In Sao Paulo, the state government has only just begun to draw up a model on how to privatise the energy sector which will comprise the bulk of the privatisation programme.

Sao Paulo's Energy Secretary David Zylbersztajn estimates selling off electricity firms Cesp, Eletropaulo and CPFL, as well as gas company Comgas will generate just under $20 billion in receipts. The rest will come from the sale of hotels and resorts, state warehouse firm Ceagesp and concessions to private firms in the transport and infrastructure sectors.

The plan is to restructure Sao Paulo's energy sector by creating 20 smaller generating and distribution firms, which will be privatised, and one transmission entity which will remain in state hands. The state also intends to retain "golden shares" in the generating and distribution units.
It hopes to sell one of the smaller electricity companies by the end of the year with the rest coming in 1997.

Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo are not the only states in Brazil to sell off their assets to help clean up their books, but their privatisation programmes are the most lucrative and they serve as an example to the others.
On a federal level, Brazil's government hopes to earn at least a record $9.25 billion in privatisation receipts in 1997.
RIO IS MORE CONDUCIVE TO PRIVATISATION
Some privatisation buffs believe the atmosphere in Rio is more conducive to privatisation and involves fewer political risks than in Sao Paulo.

"The perception of Rio's state governor is that privatisation is good publicity for him in the future. Major players in the privatisation process are in Rio, like the BNDES (National Development Bank)," said Banco Graphus managing Director Sergio Zendron. "This creates a better atmosphere."
He said Sao Paulo's legislative assembly was more resistant to change, especially with the Labour Party and trade unions pressuring politicians to hold on to state companies.

Another banker, who did not want to be named, did not anticipate any change in Sao Paulo's privatisation momentum until a new governor took over in 1998. He said it was not in Governor Mario Covas' interest to speed up privatisation at the end of his mandate, which would only allow his successor to reap the benefits.

"Sao Paulo's privatisation programme is half-hearted," he said. "Sao Paulo does not really believe in privatisation. Its way of solving its liquidity problems is not to pay the bills. Sao Paulo is like a bankrupt millionaire."
BANERJ ILLUSTRATES RIO'S PRIVATISATION ZEAL
Bozano, Simonsen's Vasconcelos said the pace with which Rio sought to privatise Banerj illustrated its privatisation zeal.

Only five months after launching its privatisation programme in August 1995 Rio state took the first steps to prepare Banerj for privatisation. In January, it placed Banerj, the most serious drain on the public purse at roughly $50 million a month, under Bozano, Simonsen's private management with the aim to clean up its books ahead of a sell-off.

Only recently, Rio state proved to be ahead in the game yet again by proposing a plan for solving Banerj's debt problem to the Central Bank which was later used as a model for the government's own rescue plan for state banks.
Rio submitted a request to the Central Bank for roughly $3 billion to cover Banerj's debts of $2.5 billion and the state's debts to the bank of $500 million.
The government rescue plan for indebted state banks offers loans to refinance 100 percent of the banks' debts to those states which privatise their institutions.

"The state has fulfilled its duty in handing Banerj over to private management," said Rio state Planning Secretary Marco Aurelio Alencar. "The decision is now in the hands of the Central Bank so that Banerj can be put up for sale."
Alencar said Banerj's privatisation model could be published as early as next month, with the bank going on sale in December.

Meanwhile, Sao Paulo's attempts to solve the problems of its heavily indebted bank Banco do Estado de Sao Paulo (Banespa) have stalled, and the state has shown no strong signs of wanting to privatise the bank with debts of $18 billion.
Zendron believes Brazil's Central Bank, which is currently administering Banespa, will eventually come up with a solution along the lines of Banerj.
"This reduces the political costs," he said. "It is easier to sack people and restructure the bank under private management than under state control."
